EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Introduction

The Brandon Water Treatment Plant (Brandon WTP) is subject to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Risk Management Program specified under 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 68 in conjunction with the use of chlorine at the facility for water disinfection. In recognition of the EPA Risk Management requirements, a Risk Management Program (RMP) Plan has been developed to maintain compliance with the components of the program.

Through the development of the RMP Plan, Brandon WTP staff has completed a comprehensive review of the risk associated with the regulated process, water chlorination, at its facility.  Additionally, staff has completed an Offsite Consequence Analysis and has developed and implemented a prevention program to promote safe operation of the regulated process.  The facility has also updated emergency response procedures and initiated communication with local authorities to form a cooperative response procedure for potential releases from the facility.  The prevention program focuses on training employees in safe operating and maintenance procedures and to recognize the potential hazards associated with the regulated chemical and processes.

Background

The Brandon WTP retains two (2) chlorine cylinders, each with the capacity of one (1) ton of chlorine gas, for a maximum combined storage of 4,000 pounds onsite for water disinfection. The use and/or storage of chlorine, which is classified as a hazardous chemical under federal standards, at the WTP causes the facility to be subject to federal requirements related to the protection of public health and safety, as well as worker safety. The EPA Risk Management Program specifies a threshold quantity of 2,500 pounds for RMP regulation. 

Chlorine containers are stored in the chlorine room, which is located in the northwest corner of the facility and is equipped with a ventilation system. The chlorine room and its components are visually inspected

at least once per day during operation. When the system is not in operation, the chlorination system equipment is off and all related process valves are closed. The door to the chlorine room is kept locked at all times.  Chlorine is a toxic gas stored as a liquid under pressure.  Its boiling point is 29.4?F.  Chlorine is irritating and corrosive to the eyes, skin, and respiratory tract and reacts violently with easily oxidized materials.  Contact with evaporating chlorine or equipment releasing flashing chlorine can cause frostbite burns.  Chlorine gas is heavier than air and will travel along the ground and fill low spaces and pits by displacing air.  One (1) ton chlorine containers are welded steel tanks with removable steel protective caps over the container valves.  They are built to meet Federal specifications and are regularly inspected and pressure tested in accordance with Federal regulations.




Management System

A management system which assigns responsibility for each component of the RMP has been instituted. This procedure will also be reviewed periodically and updated to reflect changes in responsibilities at the facility.

Offsite Consequence Analysis

The Hazard Assessment portion of the RMP Plan was developed to comply with the EPA Risk Management Program requirements. The Brandon WTP RMP staff has studied their chlorination system and the potential hazards it presents onsite and offsite.  The results of this analysis are presented in Section 3.0  Hazard Assessment, and include an Offsite Consequence Analysis, which is composed of a Worst-Case and Alternative (most likely) Case Scenario, and an Accident History.  

Worst-Case Scenario

Although the EPA acknowledges that the Worst-Case Scenario is not a likely scenario, a scenario was formulated to alert the public to the worst release possible. The Worst-Case Scenario for this facility involves the release of 2,000 pounds of gaseous chlorine (the entire contents of one (1) container) directly int

o the atmosphere over a 10-minute period. Due to the location of the facility in an urban setting, the analysis estimated that a release of this magnitude would create a radius of influence of 1.3 miles.  The radius of influence represents the distance the chlorine plume would travel from the facility, under assumed meteorological conditions, before the concentration is reduced below the toxic endpoint.  The EPAs RMP Offsite Consequence Analysis Guidance states the toxic endpoint concentration is that below which it is believed that nearly all individuals could be exposed for up to one hour without experiencing or developing irreversible or other serious health effects or symptoms that could impair an individuals ability to take protective action.  A population of approximately 7,020 people resides within the 1.3 mile radius of influence.  The EPA requires that the radius of influence be calculated considering a wind speed of 1.5 meters per second, or 3.4 miles per hour.  Historically, the average wind speed in the vicinity of Brandon is approximately 9.5 miles per hour; thus, a release would likely disperse at a faster rate than estimated under the assumed conditions.

Alternative Case Scenario

An alternative, or most likely scenario, was also developed as part of the plan.  This scenario involves a release occurring inside the chlorine room. The Brandon WTP utilizes a vacuum-operated chlorination system.  The vacuum system is, for all practical purposes, virtually fail-safe. A pressure regulating valve is installed directly onto the chlorine container, between the container and the chlorinator.  For this valve to open, a vacuum must be present on the chlorinator side of the valve.  The vacuum is created by water passing through the ejector on the chlorinator.  When a vacuum is present and the valve is open, gaseous chlorine may be drawn from the container, through the valve, into the chlorinator, and then injected into the water.  In the absence of a vacuum

on the chlorinator side of the valve, the valve closes, and chlorine cannot escape through the valve on the container.  In the event of equipment failure on the chlorinator side of the valve, the valve is designed to immediately close due to the absence of a vacuum.  Because the regulating valve is attached directly to the chlorine container, the most likely potential escape route for chlorine gas from the container is between the valve stem on the container and the pressure-regulating valve.  The chlorine cylinders are stored within ChlorTainers which, in the event of a leak, close off to contain the chlorine gas within the ChlorTainer.

The Alternative Case Scenario modeled for this facility involves a leak from the lead gasket between the regulating valve and the chlorine container. Each time a new container is connected to the system, a new gasket is installed. Although the gasket is checked for leaks immediately after installation, the Alternate Case Scenario assumes a small leak is not detected prior to shutdown of the system at the end of the day. The leak continues throughout the night and the entire contents of the vessel are released over a period of 134 minutes (15 lbs/minute).  Because the vessel is inside the building with the door closed, the room acts as a passive mitigation measure and contains the release.  The radius of influence for this release is 0.1 miles, which includes approximately seven (7) single family residences, one (1) municipal pool, two (2) tennis courts, and three (3) baseball fields. The assumed population affected by the Alternative Case Scenario is 250 people based on an estimate for the number of residences contained within the radius of influence. The chlorine room has a chlorine monitor with the sensor near the floor that will alarm in the event of a chlorine release to notify personnel and mitigate the consequences. In recognition of this potential release, the Brandon WTP will integrate Risk Management Program training with

its existing training program. Increased employee awareness of the consequences of even a small release is expected to further reduce the likelihood of such a scenario occurring.

In order to reduce the chance of a chlorine leak from an on-line chlorine cylinder the Brandon WTP has each cylinder stored inside of a ChlorTainer. The ChlorTainer is a sealed vessel that completely encapsulates a chlorine cylinder and is able to contain a full cylinder leak.  In addition, if a leak occurs the Brandon WTP operations is able to still utilize the chlorine from the ChlorTainer without opening the vessel.  This allows the WTP to consume the chlorine that has leaked out of the cylinder but is still contained in the ChlorTainer vessel without the release of chlorine into the atmosphere. 

Accident History

The Brandon WTP has not had an incident in the past five (5) years that resulted in injury onsite or offsite. The WTP management is committed to ongoing employee training to increase awareness of the potential hazards associated with the chlorination process and to further reduce the likelihood of future accidents which may result in injury or damage to equipment or property.







Prevention Program

The Prevention Program portion of the RMP Plan was developed to comply with the EPA Risk Management Program requirements. The intent of the Prevention Program is to document procedures within the facility that promote safe operation of the regulated process and reduce the potential for an uncontrolled release of the regulated substance (chlorine gas).  Components of the Prevention Program include:

	Safety Information
	Hazard Review (HR)
	Operating Procedures
	Training
	Maintenance
	Compliance Audits
	Third Party Audits
	Incident Investigation
	Employee Participation

Safety information, such as Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) and equipment specifications have been compiled and attached to the RMP Plan for easy access by employees.  This information specifies the safe opera

ting limits for regulated process equipment and lists codes and standards that apply to the equipment.  Instruction manuals for regulated process equipment are also attached to this section.

A Hazard Review has been conducted by site personnel to identify potential hazards associated with the chemical, process, and procedure at the site. A HR will be performed every five (5) years, or prior to implementation of a new or changed process.

Operating procedures relating to normal and emergency operations of the regulated process have been updated and compiled in the RMP Plan.  Maintenance procedures have been compiled in a similar fashion.  These procedures will be reviewed periodically and updated as necessary.

A training policy has been developed and training records have been reviewed and updated to reflect the status of all current employees.  New employee and refresher training will be provided periodically and documented in an effort to maintain safe operating and maintenance procedures.  Refresher training will be conducted every three (3) years, at a minimum.  The Brandon WTP will document all training.

A maintenance program has been developed for maintaining the mechanical integrity of process equipment associated with the regulated process. The maintenance program addresses equipment testing, preventative maintenance schedules, and personnel training.

A compliance review policy has been developed and compliance audits, designed to review the facilitys compliance with the program requirements, will be conducted every three (3) years.  The audits examine the components of the RMP Plan and the implementation of each component.  
A compliance review policy has been developed for third-party audits, designed to review the facilitys compliance with the program requirements. Third-party audits will be conducted when an accidental release occurs or an implementing agency requires a third-party audit due to conditions that could lead to an accidental release (ne

ar miss) or when a previous third-party failed to meet the competency or independence requirements.

An incident investigation procedure has been developed to aid in instituting corrective actions resulting from an incident and to prevent future incidents from occurring.  This procedure establishes a timeline for completion of an incident investigation and documents any procedure changes resulting from the investigation.

An employee participation plan was developed so that a plan of action is in place regarding employee consultation and access to safety and hazard information related to the regulated chlorine process.  All employees are allowed access to this information.

Emergency Response

Although the potential for a release exists, the Brandon WTP has determined that the chlorination system is safe by industry standards and that the potential for a release from the facility is very small.  The facility is working with local authorities to prepare emergency responders in the event of a major release.  WTP staff are not trained to respond to releases other than those that can be stopped by closing a valve and will not enter the room to stop a chlorine release if the chlorine concentration is estimated to be above safe levels.  The Brandon WTP will work with the Minnehaha County Emergency Management Department to coordinate response to a release.  A contact checklist is utilized to ensure the proper contacts are made in the case of an emergency, including at the local (fire department, county emergency planning, etc.), state (South Dakota Emergency Management), and federal levels, as necessary.  The results of the Offsite Consequence Analysis have been communicated to the necessary emergency response organizations.

Updates

Periodic updates to portions of the RMP are specified in the Risk Management Program and are listed in individual sections, if applicable.  Re-submission of an updated RMP must be no later than five (5) years after the postmark date of the pr

s, then a third-party audit is required; and 
	If a change occurs that no longer subjects the facility to the Risk Management Program regulations, then a revised registration which indicates the facility is no longer subject to the program be submitted within six (6) months of the implemented change.

There are also additional requirements for the availability of RMP information to the public as well as updating the public via different required platforms as outlined in 40 CFR Part 68

Conclusion

In summary, the City of Brandon is confident that although the potential for a chlorine release that could affect the public or the environment exists, it is slight.  The facility is committed to comprehensive employee training and communication with offsite responders in the event of a major chlorine release.  The facility has examined the hazards associated with the regulated process, identified additional safety measures, and set a schedule for implementation of those safety measures.  The Brandon WTP staff intends to use the Risk Management Program as a means to operate more safely and efficiently and to communicate more effectively with offsite responders and the public it serves.
